name: Yusuf Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the garage behind the petrol station on the ring road. Two bays, me and Mr Okafor, who owns it, plus his nephew on Saturdays. I do a lot of the basic stuff: oil, filters, tyres, getting cars ready for their yearly safety test. I like that it's simple, you see the problem, you fix it, the customer pays. What wears me out is when Mr Okafor's away and people ring asking for prices I don't know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house, three of us, with a kitchen that's always a mess. I send my mum a bit each month, which is why there's never much left. I've got maybe a week and a half of money saved, if that. The nearest other garage that'd take me is two buses away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave the cars alone. People make a lot of noise about computers and then nothing happens. I'd say that at the counter to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I was worried before any of this. The landlord wants to build flats where the garage is, AI or not. The petrol station's lease is up in two years. If that happens, the garage goes, and I don't know where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like normal and keep my head down. I'd try to put a bit more by, maybe skip the football on a Saturday, which is twenty quid with the bus. I'd ask Mr Okafor about the lease, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, honestly, but not about robots. About the flats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe ask about the lease. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Mr Okafor doesn't like being asked about money. He'd tell me when he knows, I think. He's fair like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the garage closed, what would you do the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walk round every garage and tyre place I could get to on the bus and ask. Then the warehouses, I suppose. I'd keep sending my mum something even if it was less.

say: Cars should be **left alone**, and computers make noise then nothing happens.
I'd say that at the **counter** to anyone asking.
think: The petrol station's **lease ends** in two years, and the landlord wants flats.
If the garage goes, I have **nowhere obvious** to go.
do: Carry on as normal and **keep my head down** at work.
Skip **Saturday football** to save about twenty pounds a week.
Maybe ask Mr Okafor about the **lease**, though probably not.
feel: **Worried**, but about the flats, not robots.
S0.quote: I was worried before any of this. The landlord wants to build flats where the garage is, AI or not.
fieldNote: Yusuf's main threat is a **property lease**, unrelated to AI.
He supports **his mother** from a low wage, so savings stay near zero.
He avoids hard conversations with his boss, trusting him to be **fair**.

steps.text: Keep doing oil, filters and tyres at the ring road garage
Stop going to Saturday football to save the bus and ticket money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the big places, not us. A two-bay garage behind a petrol station doesn't need a computer brain. I'd say that and I'd mostly believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't know. If the big chains get cheaper with their software, our customers go there, and Mr Okafor can't afford me. And if the computer tells people what's wrong with their car before they come in, they'll know if I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do much differently, to be honest. I'd keep working and try to get faster. I'm not going to start with AI apps, I don't trust them and I don't have the patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit stupid, like everyone else knows something I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the customer would know if you're guessing. Are you guessing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, yeah, on the electrical stuff. I swap a part and see if it fixes it. Mr Okafor tells me off for it because it costs the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let Mr Okafor bring in a computer system if he wanted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's his garage, so yeah. I'd learn the bits I had to. But I wouldn't be the one asking for it.

say: AI is for **big places** like the chains, not a two-bay garage like ours.
A small garage behind a petrol station doesn't need a **computer brain**.
think: Cheaper **chains** could take our customers, and then Mr Okafor can't afford me.
Customers with AI diagnosis would know when I'm **guessing**.
do: **Keep working** and try to get faster at the basics.
**Avoid AI apps**, because I don't trust them or have the patience.
Learn only the parts of any new system the **boss requires**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit stupid, as if everyone knows something I don't.
S1.quote: If the computer tells people what's wrong with their car before they come in, they'll know if I'm guessing.
fieldNote: Yusuf admits he sometimes **swaps parts and hopes**, which AI diagnosis would expose.
He is **resistant** but pragmatic: he'd follow his boss rather than lead.
Chains getting cheaper is his main route to **losing the job**.

steps.text: Keep working on basic services and try to get faster
Wait to see if Mr Okafor brings in a system before learning it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing, I'd just go quiet. Maybe that the politicians should have seen it coming, all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished. The pricing and the diagnosing go in 2028 and that's the part Mr Okafor does, so he'd need me even less. Then robots in 2031 and I'm thirty-one with a week of savings and no other skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd keep going to work as long as there was work. I'd probably ask my uncle, who drives a taxi, if there's anything, but taxis are going too, aren't they. I'd have to stop sending my mum money, and that's the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like panic. Like the floor's gone and I can't see where to step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start doing now, in the next two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't think of anything. Courses cost money and I don't know what to study. Everyone says learn computers, but the computers are the thing taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at first. I'd just send less and say work was quiet. She'd worry more than me, and she's got her own bills.

say: I'd probably **go quiet** and say nothing at work or online.
Maybe that **all the politicians**, from every side, should have seen it coming.
think: Pricing and diagnosing go in **2028**, so Mr Okafor needs me even less.
By **2031** robots arrive and I've a week of savings and no other skill.
do: Keep going to work **as long as** there's work.
Ask my **uncle the taxi driver** about any openings.
Stop **sending money** to my mum, which hurts most.
feel: **Panic**, like the floor's gone and I can't see where to step.
S2.quote: Everyone says learn computers, but the computers are the thing taking it.
fieldNote: Yusuf has **no plan** and no money to make one, which fits panicked.
He would hide cutting **his mother's support**, showing shame and protectiveness.
He finds the usual advice to retrain **circular and useless**.

steps.text: Keep turning up at the garage while work lasts
Ask his uncle the taxi driver about other work
Cut the money he sends his mum each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so somebody had better have a plan. Not left or right, just something that works. I'd probably say it at the counter more than online, I'm not really online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is maybe enough for me to find something, if I knew what to look for. The thinking stuff goes in 2031, and robots for the hands-on bit in 2034. So I've got the most time on the tyres and oil side, which is daft, because that's the cheapest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait a year or two and see what other mechanics are doing. If someone I know goes and gets a job fixing the robots, I'd follow. I'd try to save something each month, even if it's thirty quid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, still. Less than the fast one, but scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wait a year or two. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Mr Okafor gets a computer that does the quoting. And whether the big tyre place on the retail park starts laying people off. That's how I'd know it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the garage closed for the flats. Then I'd have no choice.

say: We've got **five years**, so somebody had better have a plan.
It shouldn't be **left or right**, just something that works.
think: Five years might be enough, **if I knew** what to look for.
The **cheapest work**, tyres and oil, is the work that lasts longest.
do: Wait **a year or two** and follow what other mechanics do.
Save **thirty pounds a month** if I can manage it.
Watch the **retail park** tyre place for layoffs as a warning.
feel: **Scared**, less than with the fast one, but still scared.
S3.quote: I've got the most time on the tyres and oil side, which is daft, because that's the cheapest work.
fieldNote: Yusuf sees the irony that the **cheapest hands-on work** survives longest.
He'd only move when **someone he knows** shows a route first.
The **flats plan** would force his hand more than AI would.

steps.text: Watch whether the retail park tyre place starts laying people off
Save thirty pounds a month from his wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not panic. People said cars would drive themselves by now and they don't. I'd say get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years and then three more for robots is thirteen years. I'd be forty. I can probably work till then if the garage survives the flats, and if not, I'd find another garage in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and maybe, once it's clearer, do a course. Probably something electrical, because everyone says the new cars are all electric. I'd also try to get a proper room in a better place, maybe with a mate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, but it sits there in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once it's clearer. What does clear look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Mr Okafor says we need it. Or when the jobs online all say electric. I don't want to waste money on the wrong course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger lad starting in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the electric side early, and don't wait for someone to tell you. I'd tell a younger lad that and then probably not do it myself.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so let's not panic.
People said cars would **drive themselves** by now, and they don't.
think: Thirteen years until robots means I'd be **forty**.
If the garage survives the **flats**, I can probably work until then.
do: Keep working and do an **electrical course** once it's clearer.
Look for a **better room** shared with a mate.
Wait for the boss or **job adverts** to show which course matters.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the worry sitting at the back of my head.
S4.quote: Learn the electric side early, and don't wait for someone to tell you. I'd tell a younger lad that and then probably not do it myself.
fieldNote: The flats lease keeps Yusuf **anxious** even with a decade of warning.
He'd advise others to act early but admits **he won't**, a candid gap.
He fears **wasting money** on the wrong course more than acting late.

steps.text: Wait for Mr Okafor or job adverts before picking a course
Take an electrical vehicle course once demand is clear
Move into a better shared room with a friend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, and I don't have a plan or the money to make one. What would help is someone telling me straight which course leads to a real job, and paying for it, because I can't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who send money home. Lots of us do. When you cut back, you're not just cutting yourself, you're cutting your family.

headlineQuote: When you cut back, you're not just cutting yourself, you're cutting your family.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** junior at a two-bay garage behind a petrol station.
He rents a room, sends **money to his mother**, and has about a week and a half saved.
He never uses AI and **waits** for his boss or others to show the way first.
A planned **flats development** on the garage site worries him in every scenario.
His mood runs from anxious to **panicked** in the 2028 scenario, where he has no plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him with no plan, no savings and no other skill.
whatWouldHelp: Someone to say **which course** leads to real work, and to **pay** for it.
